Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

items.content: Type: Pseudo-stratified Columnar | Location: Respiratory passage and ducts of many glands | Structure: Similar to columnar epithelium but all the cells are not of similar height | Function: Protection, secretion and movement of mucous [mucus].

teacher_understanding.question: How does this row compare pseudostratified with columnar epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: It retains a columnar-like appearance, but the cells do not have similar heights.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the distinction between pseudostratified and genuinely stratified epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Pseudostratified epithelium is one layer whose differing cell heights and nuclear levels suggest several layers; genuinely stratified epithelium has multiple cell layers. In pseudostratified epithelium, the cells contact the basement membrane although some do not reach the free surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the book locate it and what jobs does it list?
teacher_understanding.answer: In respiratory passages and ducts of many glands, with protection, secretion and mucus movement as listed functions.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the respiratory example link secretion to protection?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mucus traps inhaled particles, while cilia in ciliated respiratory epithelium move the mucus toward the throat. This is a respiratory example, not a claim that every pseudostratified lining has cilia.

items.exam_note: Trap: apparent layering does not establish true stratification; distinguish mucus from cilia that move it.

items.content: Type: Keratinised | Location, as printed: The outer or apical layer of the cell | Structure: Mostly dead and devoid of nucleus and cytoplasm. The cytoplasm gets replaced by keratin, which makes the layer waterproof | Function: Protection against abrasion.

teacher_understanding.question: What characterises the keratinised layer in this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: The outer cells are described as mostly dead, lacking nucleus and cytoplasm, with keratin replacing the cytoplasm and making the layer waterproof.

teacher_understanding.question: What location wording does the book provide?
teacher_understanding.answer: It prints 'The outer or apical layer of the cell' rather than naming an organ.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a learner understand the location biologically?
teacher_understanding.answer: Keratinisation concerns the superficial cells of an epithelial tissue; the skin's epidermis is the familiar example. It is not a separate outer tissue layer inside an individual cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is keratinisation useful at an exposed surface?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tough keratin-rich outer covering resists rubbing and reduces water loss. The protection belongs to the surface layer, not to a claim that the entire epithelium is dead.

items.exam_note: Associate keratinisation with abrasion protection; do not generalise superficial dead cells to the whole tissue.

items.type_note: The row describes a tissue's layered arrangement, sites and functions; its stretch response is a supporting mechanism rather than the whole item's type.

teacher_understanding.question: What is transitional epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Also called urothelium, it is a stratified lining that can expand or contract and change its apparent cell shape with stretching.

teacher_understanding.question: Which sites does this table list?
teacher_understanding.answer: Urinary bladder, urethra and ureter.

teacher_understanding.question: When does its appearance change?
teacher_understanding.answer: Without stretching, cells are described as cuboidal; when the organ stretches, the tissue becomes compressed and cells appear irregular and squamous-shaped.

teacher_understanding.question: How does its structure meet the functions listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stretches to accommodate different liquid volumes, while its barrier and tight junctions prevent reabsorption of toxic substances.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must a bladder lining combine flexibility with a barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: The bladder fills and empties, so its lining must tolerate changing size without allowing urine constituents to leak readily back into surrounding tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the table's reference to urethra mean its entire length is urothelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Urothelium occurs in the proximal urethral region; other epithelial types line more distal regions. The table's site list is simplified.

items.exam_note: High-value pairing: urothelium—urinary tract—stretch plus barrier; flattened appearance during stretching does not make it simple squamous epithelium.

items.content: Connective Tissues
items.exam_note: Introduces the next tissue group.

items.content: Connects body parts

teacher_understanding.question: What role is introduced here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Connective tissue links body parts so they can form an organised body rather than remain separate structures.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can this connecting role be seen?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tendons connect muscles to bones, while ligaments connect bones to other bones.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a connecting tissue transmit a pull?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its strong extracellular fibres carry tension between the attached structures, as when a tendon transfers muscle pull to bone.

prerequisites: tissue as a group of cells
items.exam_note: Connect function with familiar connective-tissue examples; tendon–ligament examples are explanatory additions.

why_chain.step: Body parts need attachments to function together.

unpack.example_or_place: Outside example: tendon between muscle and bone.
unpack.consequence: Introduces a supporting and linking role distinct from a surface lining.
unpack.visual_verb: Join two body parts with a connective band.
unpack.level_extra: Keep tendon and ligament attachments distinct.

items.content: Prevents organs from getting displaced by body movement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do organs need support during body movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Walking, bending and other movements exert forces on internal structures, so organs need attachments and supporting tissue to limit unwanted shifting.

teacher_understanding.question: How does connective tissue help?
teacher_understanding.answer: It provides a supportive framework and attachments that hold organs in their anatomical relationships while permitting normal movement.

teacher_understanding.question: What outcome does the book state?
teacher_understanding.answer: It prevents organs from being displaced by body movement.

items.exam_note: Interpret prevention of displacement as support, not complete immobilisation.

unpack.visual_verb: Move the body while supporting bands keep organs positioned.

items.content: Acts like binding, supporting and packing material.

teacher_understanding.question: How do binding, supporting and packing differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Binding links structures, supporting helps maintain their position or shape, and packing fills spaces around or between structures.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can this packing role be visualised?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loose connective tissue occurs beneath the skin and around structures such as vessels and nerves.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a tissue provide these roles without being a solid block of cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells occupy an extracellular material containing fibres and ground substance; that material can link, support and fill spaces.

items.exam_note: Understand the three functions rather than memorising them as interchangeable words.

items.content: Cells are loosely spaced.

teacher_understanding.question: What does loosely spaced mean here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells are separated rather than forming a tightly packed continuous sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the intervening material located?
teacher_understanding.answer: Between the cells; the next bullet identifies it as intercellular matrix in which the cells are embedded.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is loose spacing not the same as useless empty space?
teacher_understanding.answer: The intervening matrix performs much of the tissue's supporting and mechanical work, so the non-cellular part is functional material.

items.exam_note: Distinguish spaced connective-tissue cells from closely packed epithelial cells.

items.content: Cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix.

teacher_understanding.question: What is intercellular matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is material outside and between cells, rather than the cytoplasm inside a cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the cells relative to this matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells are embedded within it, so the matrix surrounds and separates them.

teacher_understanding.question: How does matrix contribute to connective-tissue function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its composition and fibres influence strength, flexibility and consistency, helping explain how different connective tissues support or connect structures.

items.exam_note: Matrix is extracellular, not cytoplasm; connect matrix properties with function.

unpack.consequence: The matrix can differ greatly in consistency, as the next bullet states.

items.content: Matrix may be jelly, fluid, dense or rigid.

teacher_understanding.question: Which matrix consistencies are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Jelly-like, fluid, dense and rigid forms are listed as possible matrix states.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these descriptions differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: A fluid can flow; a jelly-like material is soft and gel-like; a dense matrix is closely packed with material such as fibres; a rigid matrix strongly resists deformation. These are descriptive properties rather than necessarily mutually exclusive formal classes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can one tissue family have such different consistencies?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its members perform different jobs: a flowing medium enables transport, while a rigid material provides firm support. Matrix composition varies accordingly.

teacher_understanding.question: What familiar examples clarify fluid, dense and rigid matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood has fluid plasma, tendons have dense fibrous matrix, and bone has rigid mineralised matrix.

items.exam_note: Trap: connective tissues are not uniformly solid or soft; blood and bone illustrate opposite consistencies.

teacher_understanding.question: Which matrix consistencies are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Jelly-like, fluid, dense and rigid forms are listed as possible matrix states.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these descriptions differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: A fluid can flow; a jelly-like material is soft and gel-like; a dense matrix is closely packed with material such as fibres; a rigid matrix strongly resists deformation. These are descriptive properties rather than necessarily mutually exclusive formal classes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can one tissue family have such different consistencies?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its members perform different jobs: a flowing medium enables transport, while a rigid material provides firm support. Matrix composition varies accordingly.

teacher_understanding.question: What familiar examples clarify fluid, dense and rigid matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood has fluid plasma, tendons have dense fibrous matrix, and bone has rigid mineralised matrix.

replace_items.exam_note: Trap: connective tissues are not uniformly solid or soft; blood and bone illustrate opposite consistencies.

items.content: Type: Keratinised | Location, as printed: The outer or apical layer of the cell | Structure: Mostly dead and devoid of nucleus and cytoplasm. The cytoplasm gets replaced by keratin, which makes the layer waterproof | Function: Protection against abrasion.

teacher_understanding.question: What characterises the keratinised layer in this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: The outer cells are described as mostly dead, lacking nucleus and cytoplasm, with keratin replacing the cytoplasm and making the layer waterproof.

teacher_understanding.question: What location wording does the book provide?
teacher_understanding.answer: It prints 'The outer or apical layer of the cell' rather than naming an organ.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a learner understand the location biologically?
teacher_understanding.answer: Keratinisation concerns the superficial cells of an epithelial tissue; the skin's epidermis is the familiar example. It is not a separate outer tissue layer inside an individual cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is keratinisation useful at an exposed surface?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tough keratin-rich outer covering resists rubbing and reduces water loss. The protection belongs to the surface layer, not to a claim that the entire epithelium is dead.

items.exam_note: Associate keratinisation with abrasion protection; do not generalise superficial dead cells to the whole tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What is transitional epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Also called urothelium, it is a stratified lining that can expand or contract and change its apparent cell shape with stretching.

teacher_understanding.question: Which sites does this table list?
teacher_understanding.answer: Urinary bladder, urethra and ureter.

teacher_understanding.question: When does its appearance change?
teacher_understanding.answer: Without stretching, cells are described as cuboidal; when the organ stretches, the tissue becomes compressed and cells appear irregular and squamous-shaped.

teacher_understanding.question: How does its structure meet the functions listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stretches to accommodate different liquid volumes, while its barrier and tight junctions prevent reabsorption of toxic substances.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must a bladder lining combine flexibility with a barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: The bladder fills and empties, so its lining must tolerate changing size without allowing urine constituents to leak readily back into surrounding tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the table's reference to urethra mean its entire length is urothelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Urothelium occurs in the proximal urethral region; other epithelial types line more distal regions. The table's site list is simplified.

items.exam_note: High-value pairing: urothelium—urinary tract—stretch plus barrier; flattened appearance during stretching does not make it simple squamous epithelium.

unpack.example_or_place: Outside example: lining of the mouth.
unpack.consequence: Protection can be inferred from layering without assuming every layer has flat cells.
unpack.visual_verb: Stack layers and flatten the top.
unpack.level_extra: The drawing alone does not establish keratinisation.

items.content: Stratified cuboidal: label beneath two visible layers of cube-like cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement does the drawing display?
teacher_understanding.answer: Two visible cell layers with cube-like surface cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which clue separates it from simple cuboidal?
teacher_understanding.answer: The additional layer: the simple cuboidal drawing has one layer.

teacher_understanding.question: Why inspect surface shape as well as layer count?
teacher_understanding.answer: Layer count distinguishes simple from stratified, while surface-cell shape distinguishes stratified cuboidal from other stratified epithelia.

items.exam_note: Use both layers and surface shape in identification.

terms.plain_meaning: कई परतों वाली lining जिसके ऊपर के cells घन जैसे हों
terms.everyday_image: पासों की दो कतारें एक के ऊपर एक

why_chain.step: A duct lining may need protection; multiple layers add protective depth.

unpack.example_or_place: Outside example: ducts of sweat glands.
unpack.consequence: Same cell shape does not mean the same epithelial type if layer count differs.
unpack.visual_verb: Stack two rows of cubes.
unpack.level_extra: The figure shows two layers; do not turn that into a universal layer-number rule.

items.content: Pseudostratified columnar: label beneath tall cells with nuclei at different heights, producing an apparently layered pattern.

teacher_understanding.question: What visual pattern does this drawing emphasise?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tall cells contain nuclei at different levels rather than in one neat horizontal row.

teacher_understanding.question: Which upper-table row corresponds to this drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Pseudo-stratified Columnar, described there as having unequal cell heights.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the apparent layering misleading?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cells can share contact with one basement membrane while their nuclei occupy different heights; apparent nuclear rows are not separate true layers.

items.exam_note: Common conceptual trap: nuclei at different levels do not make true stratification.

terms.plain_meaning: कई परतों जैसा दिखे, पर असल में वैसा न हो
terms.everyday_image: एक कतार में खड़े अलग कद के लोगों के सिर अलग ऊँचाई पर दिखना

why_chain.step: Uneven nuclear heights can mislead the viewer; tracing cell bases resolves the apparent layering.

unpack.example_or_place: Respiratory passage, as listed in the table.
unpack.consequence: Links the table's unequal heights to a visible recognition clue.
unpack.visual_verb: Highlight staggered nuclei and trace cells to their base.
unpack.level_extra: Pseudo means apparent, not genuinely multilayered.

items.content: Transitional: label above a multilayered block with large rounded superficial cells over smaller underlying cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What is visible in the transitional drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Several cell layers with broad, rounded cells at the upper surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which table entry explains this labelled drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transitional epithelia or urothelium, the stretchable urinary-tract lining.

teacher_understanding.question: How would this appearance change during stretching?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table explains that the tissue becomes compressed and cells appear irregular and squamous-shaped.

items.exam_note: The rounded surface drawing and stretched flattened state belong to the same tissue.

terms.plain_meaning: खिंचाव के साथ आकार बदलने वाली lining
terms.everyday_image: bladder भरने पर अंदर की परत का फैलना

why_chain.step: Changing urine volume requires a lining that can accommodate expansion.
The table links stretching with a flatter cell appearance.

unpack.example_or_place: Urinary bladder.
unpack.consequence: One static drawing must be linked to the changing shape described above.
unpack.visual_verb: Morph rounded surface cells into flatter cells.
unpack.level_extra: Do not reclassify the stretched tissue as simple squamous.

items.content: Connective Tissues
items.exam_note: Introduces the next tissue group.

items.content: Connects body parts

teacher_understanding.question: What role is introduced here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Connective tissue links body parts so they can form an organised body rather than remain separate structures.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can this connecting role be seen?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tendons connect muscles to bones, while ligaments connect bones to other bones.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a connecting tissue transmit a pull?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its strong extracellular fibres carry tension between the attached structures, as when a tendon transfers muscle pull to bone.

prerequisites: tissue as a group of cells
items.exam_note: Connect function with familiar connective-tissue examples; tendon–ligament examples are explanatory additions.

terms.plain_meaning: शरीर के हिस्सों को जोड़ने और सहारा देने वाले tissues
terms.everyday_image: कपड़े के हिस्सों को जोड़ती सिलाई

why_chain.step: Body parts need attachments to function together.
Connective tissue supplies such connections.

unpack.example_or_place: Outside example: tendon between muscle and bone.
unpack.consequence: Introduces a supporting and linking role distinct from a surface lining.
unpack.visual_verb: Join two body parts with a connective band.
unpack.level_extra: Keep tendon and ligament attachments distinct.

items.content: Prevents organs from getting displaced by body movement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do organs need support during body movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Walking, bending and other movements exert forces on internal structures, so organs need attachments and supporting tissue to limit unwanted shifting.

teacher_understanding.question: How does connective tissue help?
teacher_understanding.answer: It provides a supportive framework and attachments that hold organs in their anatomical relationships while permitting normal movement.

teacher_understanding.question: What outcome does the book state?
teacher_understanding.answer: It prevents organs from being displaced by body movement.

items.exam_note: Interpret prevention of displacement as support, not complete immobilisation.

terms.plain_meaning: अपनी जगह से खिसक जाना
terms.everyday_image: चलते बैग में बिना सहारे रखी बोतल का खिसकना

why_chain.step: Body movement could shift unsupported organs.
Connective-tissue support limits such displacement.

unpack.example_or_place: Internal organs remaining supported while a person walks.
unpack.consequence: Connective tissue stabilises without requiring organs to be motionless.
unpack.visual_verb: Move the body while supporting bands keep organs positioned.
unpack.level_extra: Avoid reading 'prevents' as forbidding normal organ movement.

items.content: Acts like binding, supporting and packing material.

teacher_understanding.question: How do binding, supporting and packing differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Binding links structures, supporting helps maintain their position or shape, and packing fills spaces around or between structures.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can this packing role be visualised?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loose connective tissue occurs beneath the skin and around structures such as vessels and nerves.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a tissue provide these roles without being a solid block of cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells occupy an extracellular material containing fibres and ground substance; that material can link, support and fill spaces.

items.exam_note: Understand the three functions rather than memorising them as interchangeable words.

terms.plain_meaning: हिस्सों को जोड़कर रखना
terms.everyday_image: गठरी को बाँधती डोरी

terms.plain_meaning: बीच की जगह भरकर सहारा देने वाला substance
terms.everyday_image: डिब्बे में सामान के आसपास रखी गद्दी

why_chain.step: Body structures need connections, support and filled intervening spaces.
Connective tissues serve as binding, supporting and packing material.

unpack.example_or_place: Outside example: loose connective tissue beneath skin.
unpack.consequence: Prepares the learner to understand why material between cells matters.
unpack.visual_verb: Bind, brace and fill spaces around structures.
unpack.level_extra: Link function to the matrix described in the next bullets.

items.content: Cells are loosely spaced.

teacher_understanding.question: What does loosely spaced mean here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells are separated rather than forming a tightly packed continuous sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the intervening material located?
teacher_understanding.answer: Between the cells; the next bullet identifies it as intercellular matrix in which the cells are embedded.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is loose spacing not the same as useless empty space?
teacher_understanding.answer: The intervening matrix performs much of the tissue's supporting and mechanical work, so the non-cellular part is functional material.

items.exam_note: Distinguish spaced connective-tissue cells from closely packed epithelial cells.

terms.plain_meaning: cells एक-दूसरे से कुछ दूरी पर हों
terms.everyday_image: जेली में दूर-दूर रखे फल के टुकड़े

why_chain.step: A supporting tissue needs useful material between its cells.
Connective cells are spaced within matrix rather than forming a packed surface sheet.

unpack.example_or_place: A schematic connective tissue with cells separated by matrix.
unpack.consequence: Loose spacing leads directly to the importance of intercellular matrix.
unpack.visual_verb: Separate cells and reveal material filling the gaps.
unpack.level_extra: Loose spacing is an arrangement, not a claim that all connective tissue is soft.

items.content: Cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix.

teacher_understanding.question: What is intercellular matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is material outside and between cells, rather than the cytoplasm inside a cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the cells relative to this matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells are embedded within it, so the matrix surrounds and separates them.

teacher_understanding.question: How does matrix contribute to connective-tissue function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its composition and fibres influence strength, flexibility and consistency, helping explain how different connective tissues support or connect structures.

items.exam_note: Matrix is extracellular, not cytoplasm; connect matrix properties with function.

terms.plain_meaning: cells के बाहर और उनके बीच भरा substance
terms.everyday_image: फल के टुकड़ों को चारों तरफ से घेरे जेली

why_chain.step: Separated cells need a surrounding material that helps the tissue function.
The cells are embedded in matrix, whose properties help determine the tissue's behaviour.

unpack.example_or_place: Connective tissue: zoom from several spaced cells to the material around them.
unpack.consequence: The matrix can differ greatly in consistency, as the next bullet states.
unpack.visual_verb: Highlight the material around cells while leaving their interiors uncoloured.
unpack.level_extra: Intercellular means between cells, not inside them.

items.content: Matrix may be jelly, fluid, dense or rigid.

teacher_understanding.question: Which matrix consistencies are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Jelly-like, fluid, dense and rigid forms are listed as possible matrix states.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these descriptions differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: A fluid can flow; a jelly-like material is soft and gel-like; a dense matrix is closely packed with material such as fibres; a rigid matrix strongly resists deformation. These are descriptive properties rather than necessarily mutually exclusive formal classes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can one tissue family have such different consistencies?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its members perform different jobs: a flowing medium enables transport, while a rigid material provides firm support. Matrix composition varies accordingly.

teacher_understanding.question: What familiar examples clarify fluid, dense and rigid matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood has fluid plasma, tendons have dense fibrous matrix, and bone has rigid mineralised matrix.

items.exam_note: Trap: connective tissues are not uniformly solid or soft; blood and bone illustrate opposite consistencies.

terms.plain_meaning: जिसमें substance या fibres पास-पास और खूब हों
terms.everyday_image: कसकर बुनी रस्सी

terms.plain_meaning: जो आसानी से मुड़े या दबे नहीं
terms.everyday_image: हड्डी की सख्ती

why_chain.step: Transport and firm support require different physical properties.
Differences in matrix composition allow connective tissues to meet these different needs.

unpack.example_or_place: Outside examples: blood plasma, tendon and bone.
unpack.consequence: Shared connective-tissue organisation does not imply identical consistency.
unpack.visual_verb: Flow, wobble, pull and resist bending in four contrasting panels.
unpack.level_extra: Use examples as explanatory additions, not as examples explicitly printed on this page.

items.content: Connective tissues, support and connect different tissues and organs of the body.

teacher_understanding.question: What overall identity does this statement give connective tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies them by their support and connection of other tissues and organs.

teacher_understanding.question: Which earlier statements on this page support that description?
teacher_understanding.answer: The earlier bullets describe connecting body parts, limiting organ displacement, and acting as binding, supporting and packing material.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the matrix connect this definition to tissue structure?
teacher_understanding.answer: The material surrounding connective-tissue cells supplies much of the physical framework through which support and attachment are achieved.

items.exam_note: Consolidates the defining role; use structure–function reasoning rather than repeating earlier bullets.

terms.plain_meaning: हिस्सों को टिके रहने और आकार बनाए रखने में मदद देना
terms.everyday_image: किसी सामान को थामता ढाँचा

why_chain.step: Different organs and tissues need stable relationships within the body.
Connective tissues provide support and connections between them.

unpack.example_or_place: Recall the supported organs and connected body parts in the preceding bullets.
unpack.consequence: Combines the functional bullets into the identity of this tissue group.
unpack.visual_verb: Link tissues and organs into one supported arrangement.
unpack.level_extra: A shared function does not imply one identical matrix across the family.
